questions_and_answers.question: Which of the following Hindi participles would you use to describe 'the seated man'?
How is the adjectival participle construction marked in Hindi?

answers.answer: By adding a form of हुआ to the participle.

questions_and_answers.question: Which series shows how an adjectival participle phrase can be used adverbially in the oblique singular masculine form?
In Hindi, how would you express the idea 'I have a headache'?

answers.answer: मेरा सिर दर्द कर रहा है।

questions_and_answers.question: When combining two verbs with the same subject, what marker is used to replace the ending of the first verb?
Which form is used in Hindi to indicate a planned but not necessarily completed action in the past?

answers.answer: Perfect participle plus past auxiliary था

questions_and_answers.question: According to the grammar, what does the auxiliary in 'आप गये थे न?' indicate?

answers.answer: The speaker doubts whether the listener went.
The speaker knows the listener did go.

questions_and_answers.question: Which sentence shows the verb agreeing with a direct object in the direct case?

answers.answer: आपने इस किताब को पढ़ा था।
आपको इस किताब को पढ़ना था।

questions_and_answers.question: When the verb cannot agree with the subject, what does it agree with?

answers.answer: The last verb in the sentence.

questions_and_answers.question: In the sentence 'हमने महात्मा जी के शब्द याद किये', which word loses its ability to control the verb's agreement?

articles.text:
You have met the basic structures of Hindi: the nouns, adjectives, pronouns, postpositions, verbs, and other kinds of words; the basic kinds of phrases—subject, direct object, indirect object, adverbial phrases, adjectival phrases and the verb phrases; the clause, which contains a verb phrase and possibly a variety of other phrases; and the sentence, in which several clauses may be combined. On this base you can go on to build a real command of the language. Most of the grammatical structures which you do not immediately recognize are in fact combinations of elements you already know. In this unit are a few more combinations which are frequent in both spoken and written Hindi.

Verb participles can be used as adjectives. A form of हुआ may be added to mark this adjectival construction. With the present or imperfective participle, examples include: सोती हुई लड़की – the sleeping girl; बहता हुआ पानी – the flowing water (examples in sentences 6, 7, 8). With the past or perfective participle: टूटा हुआ बटन – a broken button; बैठा हुआ अदमी – the seated man (sentences 6, 9, 16, 17); आपकी लिखी हुआ किताब – the book which you wrote; मेरी कल की पहनी हुआ जुराबें – the socks I wore yesterday (sentences 12, 13). These adjectival phrases, like any others, may be used adverbially, in the oblique singular masculine form: बैठे हुए – taking a seat; साड़ी पहनते हुए – while dressing (sentences 9, 18); साड़ियां पहनते हुए – wearing saris; टाई पहनते हुए – wearing a necktie (sentences 10, 11, 14, 15). The adverb can be repeated: चलते चलते – walking constantly; हँसते हँसते – laughing constantly (sentences 1, 4, 5, 19, 20). Expressions such as मरते मरते – on the brink of dying – and गिरते गिरते – on the brink of falling – appear in sentences 2, 3, 18.

Hindi has no verb "have". It is therefore impossible to translate "literally" any sentence that uses it. You have to stop and think what is meant. In English we say "I have two children." Hindi uses for this a possessive adjective or a का‑phrase: उनके दो बच्चे हैं – They have two children. The same pattern is used for other relatives, body parts and things you can hardly lose: उसकी एक आँख है – He has one eye. In English we say "I have a headache." In Hindi this can be "There's a pain in my head": मेरे सिर में दर्द है. Other kinds of illness are expressed with को: मुझे जुकाम है – I have a cold; मुझे बुखार था – I had a fever. Ownership is usually expressed with पास, for example: मेरे पास दो गाड़ियां थीं; हमारे पास अपना घर नहीं होगा; क्या आप लोगों के पास रहने के लिए बड़े‑बड़े मकान हैं?

When two or more verbs are used together with the same subject, the endings of all but the last can be replaced by the special marker कर. For example: जाइये देखकर देखिये – Go and see; खाना खाइए और वापस आईए – Eat and then come back. The abbreviation marker may appear as कर, के or करके. If the root of the abbreviated verb is कर, then के is the marker. For example: हम अपना काम करके गर गए – After doing our work, we went home. The subject, if mentioned, is marked by ने only if the last verb requires it: हमने गर जाकर काम किया – We went home and worked. When a series of two or more verbs are put together the abbreviation marker (कर, के or करके) can be omitted: लेकर आईए – Take it and come (bring it). This usually appears as ले आईए. Other common examples are ले जाना (carry) and ले चलना (bring along). When कर is understood, both verbs have their full meanings. Such combinations can be confusing because they look like a full verb plus a clarifier. वह खाना खा गया can mean either खाना खा कर गया – He ate and went – or it can represent the main verb खाना plus the clarifier जाना: वह सारा खाना खा गया – He ate it all up.

The difference between the meaning of the perfect participle by itself and the perfect participle plus the past auxiliary is subtle. With the past auxiliary the meaning is clearly in the past. मैं गया था will be used wherever in English 'I had gone' is appropriate, but also in many cases where 'I went' is used. The perfect participle alone often gives a suggestion of indefiniteness. It will be used in questions: क्या आप गये? – Did you go? But if the asker thinks he knows the answer, the past auxiliary is added: आप गये थे न? – You did go, didn't you? The auxiliary is also used to refer to an action that was definitely intended or planned even if not carried out: मैं नहीं गया था – I didn't go, after all. The use of the present auxiliary shows some connection with the present or the very recent past: आपने शादी की है? – Have you gotten married? If you believe that the person is not married now you might ask: शादी की थी? – Have you ever married? The past auxiliary separates the action mentioned from the present.

Verb agreement: the verb can agree only with a direct case expression. If the subject is in the direct case, the verb agrees with it. If however the subject is oblique (with को or ने) the verb may come under the control of some other direct case expression. If a direct object is present and not marked by को the verb will agree with it. If no direct expression is available, the verb reverts to its neutral masculine singular form. For example: आप यह किताब पढ़ते थे – you read this book (verb agrees with किताब); आपको यह किताब पढ़नी थी – with the oblique subject, the verb is in the neutral form; आपने यह किताब पढ़ी थी; आपने इस किताब को पढ़ा था; आपको इस किताब को पढ़ना था.

If the verb cannot agree with the subject of the sentence, it will agree with the nearest direct‑case noun (which is usually the direct object). There is one exception to this rule: a few nouns, when used with करता, lose the power to control the verb. Examples: हमने महात्मा जी के शब्द याद किये – We remembered his words; हमने अपना पाठ याद किया – We memorized our lesson; इनहोंने आपकी साड़ियां पसंद कीं – She liked your saris; इनहोंने हमारे शहर पसंद किए – He liked our cities; मैने ये चीज़ें इस्तिमाल किं – I used these things; मैने ये कमरा इस्तिमाल किया – I used this room. Normally, याद, पसंद and इस्तेमाल are nouns, but when used with करता they become transparent, allowing the effect of a preceding noun to pass through them and control the verb. Sentences such as आपकी पसंद अच्छी है – You have good taste; मेरी याद इतनी अच्छी नहीं है – My memory isn’t so good; अंग्रेजी का इस्तेमाल अच्छा नहीं – It’s bad to use English – show that the noun phrases control agreement rather than the neutral form.
